item.title: Interesting Stuff - Week 46, 2026
item.description:
This week is all about agents that remember, agents that multiply, and agents that cost less. Anthropic explains how Claude “dreams” to tidy up its memory, ships Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, and shows 1,000 Fable agents formalising Fermat’s Last Theorem in under 30 hours, coordinating through nothing fancier than a shared Postgres database. Yes, a database. My data-engineering heart is singing.

On top of that, Claude Whiteboards, Sheets and Data arrive so your work can stay in Claude, and Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley release TokenEconomizer. This plugin makes coding agents noticeably cheaper by learning from their own past sessions. Grab a coffee, and let’s dive in. The WIND section at the end is written with one foot in Cape Town and the other already in Durban.

item.title: Interesting Stuff - Week 45, 2026
item.description:
This week’s theme is making the machines (and the pipes around them) go faster. Andrej Karpathy builds a YouTube replacement in a Saturday morning with Claude Code, Anthropic shaves latency off long-running agents with message threads, and one engineering head shows how to drag CI from 40 minutes to 2 because agents never get tired of pushing.

Then we go a bit deeper down the rabbit hole: an MIT paper where an LLM reads and writes neural network weights directly, and a practical guide to the six files that turn Claude Code from a clever stranger into a teammate. Grab a coffee, and let’s dive in. There is also a WIND section at the end, because November in South Africa is conference month and my calendar looks like a bad game of Tetris.

item.title: Interesting Stuff - Week 46, 2025
item.description:
This week’s roundup explores the foundational research papers that transformed AI from an academic curiosity into production-ready technology, covering everything from the revolutionary Transformer architecture to the Model Context Protocol, which enables standardised tool integration. We examine critical performance optimisation techniques for Azure OpenAI deployments, where asynchronous programming delivers 11x speed improvements by parallelising tasks instead of processing them sequentially.

The spotlight then shifts to a paradigm-challenging analysis of why small language models with fewer than 10 billion parameters are proving architecturally superior for agentic AI systems, potentially delivering 30 times the cost savings while matching the performance of their trillion-parameter cousins on specialised tasks. Finally, I share updates from the successful .NET Conf 2025 Durban event and preview the upcoming roadshow, which will visit Cape Town and Johannesburg, where I’ll explore Model Context Protocol integration with C# and Azure AI.
